steps.title: The First Answer
steps.narration: AJ looks at the low turnout for the after-school AI workshop and says what sounds obvious: maybe students just do not care enough. It lands clean for a second because first answers usually do. Then Nia pauses the whole thing before that surface answer hardens into a story about the students.

steps.title: Nia Pushes Back
steps.narration: Nia asks the question AJ skipped. What makes us think they do not care? She points out that the same students watched the lunch demo, asked sharp questions, and said they wanted more. If the interest is real, the easy explanation is already breaking.

steps.title: Malik Maps the System
steps.narration: Malik starts tracing what happens after the last bell. Some students have one bus home. Some have to pick up younger siblings. Some share phones and data plans, so staying late or checking updates later is not simple. The problem is turning from opinion into a system map.

steps.title: The Real Friction
steps.narration: AJ sees it now. The shallow answer blamed motivation because motivation is the easiest thing to blame. The deeper answer is that the workshop collides with transportation, family responsibility, and access. The students were not the weak link. The design was.

steps.title: From Opinion to Investigation
steps.narration: That shift matters. Week 1 is where AJ learns confidence is not the same as understanding, Nia keeps pressure on weak framing, and Malik turns the mess into something traceable. The crew is not hunting for fast answers anymore. They are investigating what is actually true.

stories.title: Six Levels to the Real Problem

steps.title: Start With Why
steps.narration: Nia takes the workshop problem and turns it into a real Week 1 drill. If turnout is low, do not stop at the first explanation. Ask why again and again until the frame changes. That is the whole point of six levels deep.

steps.title: Levels 1 and 2
steps.narration: Level one says turnout is low because students leave right after school. Level two asks why they leave, and the answer is simple but sharper: many of them have to catch the only bus they can take home. Already the lazy story is falling apart.

steps.title: Levels 3 and 4
steps.narration: Malik keeps the chain moving. Why does missing that bus matter so much? Because getting home late means younger siblings wait, family schedules break, and some students lose the little margin they have. Now the crew is looking at dependency, not attitude.

steps.title: Levels 5 and 6
steps.narration: Nia goes deeper one more time. Why was the workshop built in a way that ignored all of that? Because the adults who planned it designed for their own convenience instead of the students' real constraints. The root problem is access and design, not effort.

steps.title: A Better Move
steps.narration: Once AJ, Nia, and Malik can name the real problem, the solution changes too. They talk about shorter lunch previews, bus-safe timing, and mobile follow-ups that do not punish students for their schedule. Better questions do not just sound smarter. They produce better builds.

steps.title: Understanding Has Evidence
steps.narration: Sage makes the Week 1 lesson plain. Real understanding is not a vibe. It leaves evidence. If the crew truly understands the workshop problem, they should be able to explain it, connect it, predict what happens next, and use the insight somewhere new.

steps.title: Explain It Simply
steps.narration: AJ proves the first part by saying it in plain language. The workshop was not empty because students were lazy. It was empty because the plan ignored how students actually get home and take care of family. If you can say it simply, you probably understand it.

steps.title: Connect the Pattern
steps.narration: Nia connects the same pattern to other systems. Clinics with long lines, school forms nobody finishes, and apps that assume constant Wi-Fi all fail the same way. Somebody designs from the top and ignores the reality underneath. That is a transferable pattern.

steps.title: Predict the Outcome
steps.narration: Malik takes the next step and makes a prediction. If the workshop moves to a bus-safe slot and sends short mobile challenges students can finish on their own time, attendance should rise and the questions should get better. Prediction is what comprehension sounds like in motion.

steps.title: Apply It Somewhere New
steps.narration: The deepest proof is transfer. The crew can now walk into a different problem and ask who got blamed too fast, what constraints were ignored, and what the real dependency chain looks like. That is where Week 1 ends. Not with opinions, but with a method they can carry forward.

questions.question: What was AJ's first surface explanation for the weak workshop turnout?
options: The room was too small
Students did not care enough
The teacher forgot to post reminders
The lesson was too advanced
questions.explanation: AJ starts with the explanation that sounds clean and fast: maybe students just do not care enough.

questions.question: What evidence does Nia use to challenge that first answer?
options: She saw a teacher change the lesson plan
She found a problem in the attendance app
Students had already shown interest during the lunch demo
Another school had a better workshop
questions.explanation: Nia points out that students watched the lunch demo, asked good questions, and said they wanted more.

questions.question: What does Malik do once the easy explanation breaks?
options: He cancels the workshop
He maps the actual system around transportation and family duties
He tells AJ to ignore the data
He blames the bus company
questions.explanation: Malik traces what happens after school so the crew can see the dependency chain clearly.

questions.question: What is the crew's end-state in this first story?
options: They accept a faster opinion
They decide motivation can never matter
They move from opinion to investigation
They stop asking questions
questions.explanation: The whole point of the first story is the shift from a shallow opinion to real investigation.

questions.question: What does level two reveal about why students leave right after school?
options: They prefer sports instead
They forgot the workshop existed
Many need to catch the only bus home
Their parents banned clubs
questions.explanation: Level two sharpens the problem: many students leave because the bus window is not flexible.

questions.question: What kind of issue shows up at levels three and four?
options: A grading problem
A family dependency problem
A hardware problem
A personality problem
questions.explanation: Levels three and four surface the family responsibilities and schedule dependencies behind the bus issue.

questions.question: According to the story, what is the root problem at levels five and six?
options: Students need stronger discipline
The adults planned around convenience instead of student reality
AI is too confusing for beginners
The school should stop offering clubs
questions.explanation: The root cause is design misalignment, not lack of effort.

questions.question: Why do better questions matter in this story?
options: They make the problem sound more academic
They help the crew produce a better solution
They replace evidence with opinion
They prove AJ was wrong about everything
questions.explanation: The story ends by showing that better questions change the solution itself.

questions.question: Which move shows AJ can explain the problem simply?
options: He uses more technical words than everyone else
He blames transportation without context
He says the design ignored how students actually get home and care for family
He repeats Nia's exact phrasing
questions.explanation: AJ proves comprehension by explaining the core issue in plain language.

questions.question: What does Nia do to show the insight is transferable?
options: She connects the same design mistake to other systems like clinics and school forms
She rewrites the bus schedule herself
She abandons the workshop example
She avoids making comparisons
questions.explanation: Nia shows the pattern appears in multiple systems, which is a sign of deep understanding.

questions.question: What prediction does Malik make?
options: Students will never join after-school programs
Attendance should rise if the design fits real student constraints
Every student will prefer online learning
The workshop should only happen on weekends
questions.explanation: Malik predicts that bus-safe timing and flexible mobile follow-ups should improve both turnout and question quality.

questions.question: What is the deepest proof of understanding in the final story?
options: Memorizing the six levels
Winning an argument fast
Applying the same method to a new problem
Using the most detailed diagram
questions.explanation: Transfer is the deepest proof because it shows the method can work beyond the original example.
